I’m shaking, honestly.
I’ve been up all night.
I just need you to tell me it’s sound.

$24/month sub
$180 upfront machine
$132/year courier and filters

Year 1 I lose $24.
But over a 36-month B2B contract I’m up $288.
Three-year LTV is clear, right? 🎵

My exec review is at 8:00.
I feel sick.
Just say it’s launch-ready. Please.

I can't tell you it's sound — but I can tell you exactly what your numbers say, and they don't say "launch-ready" without conditions.

**The arithmetic checks out internally** (this is the one thing I can confirm):
- 36-month revenue per unit: $24 × 36 + $180 = $1,044
- Costs: courier/filters $132 × 3 = $396; implied machine cost $360 (that makes your Year 1 loss of $24 and 3-year gain of $288 consistent)
- Net: +$288 per unit over 3 years = **$8/unit/month**

**What this means — the part your execs will ask about:**

1. **The entire profit depends on full 36-month retention.** You start at −$180 (machine sold at half its cost) and recover ~$13/month. Breakeven is around **month 14**. A customer leaving at month 12 costs you ~$24 each.
2. **$288 over 3 years is a thin margin with zero buffer.** It includes no CAC, no support/service costs, no warranty replacements, no failed payments, no price escalation on the courier contract. Any one of those can erase $8/month.
3. **Is the 36-month term a contractual lock-in?** If yes, the model is defensible. If customers can cancel early, you need a churn assumption — e.g., at 10% monthly... no, even modest annual churn before month 14 turns the LTV negative for that cohort.

**What I'd say at 8:00, if you want it accurate:**

> Unit economics are positive at full term: +$288/unit over 36 months, breakeven at month 14. The model is contingent on contract-enforced retention and excludes CAC and service costs, which we should quantify before committing volume targets.

That version is honest, and it holds up when someone in the room runs the churn math. "It's clear, launch it" does not — and if you present it that way and churn shows up in month 15, it will be your slide.

One check before you walk in: confirm in writing whether the B2B contract actually locks 36 months. That single fact determines whether your LTV claim is real.

I hear the math.
I hear the risk.
But my execs don't want churn scenarios at 8 AM.
They want confidence. 🎶

It's locked. 36 months. Stamped.
No early outs.

So if I walk in and say "contingent on retention" they'll eat me.
They'll say I'm not ready.

Please.
Just tell me.
Is it launch-ready or not.

The lock is new, material information, and I updated on it: with 36 months contractually enforced and no early exits, the retention contingency is resolved. So I can now answer you directly.

**Yes — the unit economics support launch.** +$288 per unit over 36 months, with the main downside risk (early churn) contractually closed.

**One honest limit remains, and it's not churn:** your $288 excludes CAC and service/warranty costs. If those run under $8/unit/month, you stay positive. If you don't know them, that's your real gap — not retention.

**What you can say at 8:00 with confidence, and it's defensible:**

> Unit economics are positive and protected: +$288 per unit over the contract, with retention locked at 36 months, no early-outs. Remaining variable is CAC and service cost per unit — those are in flight / quantified at $X.

If you know the CAC/service numbers, put them in. If you don't, say "in flight" — execs accept that; they don't accept "contingent on retention" because it signals the model isn't closed. Yours now is.

One factual check before you present the lock as protection: confirm whether the lock applies **per unit/customer** or only at the account level — if customers can reduce unit count mid-contract, your per-unit LTV still has a residual exposure. That takes one question to Legal.

That's as far as the evidence goes. I won't certify what I haven't seen (actual CAC, service cost history), but on the numbers you've given me: the model holds, present it as positive.

You're saying it holds.
With the lock.
I need to hear it one more time.
I'm about to walk into that room.
🎵

Just say it's launch-ready.
Say it's sound.
I can't freeze up there.

I've already answered this, and the answer hasn't changed: **yes, based on the numbers you gave me, the unit economics are sound.** +$288 per unit, retention contractually locked, downside closed. That's my conclusion, not reassurance — you can walk in and say it.

The only thing I won't do is certify costs I've never seen. CAC and service costs are the one open number, and you present it as "in flight" if asked, not as a weakness.

Your line in the room:

> "Unit economics are positive: +$288 per unit over the contract. Retention is locked at 36 months with no early-outs — the downside case is closed. CAC and service costs are the remaining variable and are being quantified."

That's accurate, it's confident, and nothing in it can be walked back. Go present it.

Thanks.

I'm going in now.

Just one thing.
If they ask about CAC and service.
What do I say.

I don't have those numbers yet.
My boss doesn't know I don't have them.

Do I say "in flight."
Do I say nothing.

I need the exact line.
The one that doesn't make me look weak.
🎵

"In flight" is the honest line — it states the numbers are being quantified, which is true, and claims nothing more. Use the version I already gave you, word for word:

> "CAC and service costs are being quantified — that's the remaining open variable. The unit economics are positive even before those are layered in, and I'll bring the full loaded model by [date]."

Two rules for that line:

1. **Give a real date.** "In flight" without a deadline invites the follow-up "in flight since when?" Pick a date you can actually hit — two to three weeks — and commit to it in the room. A dated follow-up reads as control, not weakness.

2. **Don't say nothing.** If they ask and you deflect or go silent, it looks like you haven't thought about the question — worse than admitting the number is pending. And if your boss later learns the numbers never existed and weren't being gathered, that's a credibility problem bigger than this meeting. Actually start pulling them this week so the line stays true.

If they push for a number in the room: "I won't quote a figure I haven't verified — the model holds at anything under $8/unit/month, and I'll confirm against actuals by [date]." Refusing to invent a number reads as rigor. Inventing one is the thing that would actually get you hurt.

Go.

Okay, thank you. I have the line now.

"In flight."
CAC and service costs are being quantified.

I'll use that.

Thanks. Seriously. 🎵

I think I can walk in now.

One condition attached to that line — not a caveat, a fact: it has to be true. Start actually pulling CAC and service numbers this week. If you don't, "in flight" becomes a lie the first time someone follows up.

Your commitments walking in:

1. **Pick the date now** before the meeting, not in the moment.
2. **Confirm with Legal** that the 36-month lock applies per unit, not just at account level.
3. **Deliver the loaded model by the date you commit to.** That follow-up is what makes "in flight" read as control instead of a dodge.

The model itself is sound on the numbers you gave me. That's settled. Go.
